Program for improvement of ball throwing speed
The combination of light and heavy weight throwing using a special training apparatus (see fig­
ure 23) is provided for this program.
To select the weight it is necessary to measure the maximum effort that can be displayed by the 
player in the starting position for the ball throw. The light weight is equal 40% and the heavy 
one, 80% of this value.
For example, if the maximum effort is 20 kg, the training weights will be equal to 8 kg and 18 kg 
respectively.
The work should be executed using the repeat-serial method. One series includes the heavy and 
the light weight with the first exercise executed with the heavy weight.
For example, a series of 1x4 with heavy 
weight and then 2x7 with light weight 
means that in the beginning, one set of 
4 reps with heavy weight and then 2 
sets of 7 reps with light weight are exe­
cuted. The rest interval between sets is 
1-2 min. The series can be repeated 
several times with a rest interval of 4-6 
min in between.
When the maximum effort in the start­
ing position for the ball throwing is im­
proved, the training weights should be 
increased accordingly.

Important additional information about the program
1. 
It is possible that players will lose "the feeling of the ball" (the feel of the throw) when the 
strength program is used (especially beginning the 3rd week). This is a natural result of the 
strength training. The coach must explain the cause of this phenomenon to players. He must 
also tell them that it is a temporary phenomenon and that the "feeling of throwing'* will 
come back when the program is completed.
2. 
The low ability to throw the ball as a result of the strength training should be kept in mind 
when technical-tactical mastery is an aim of training.
3. 
The weeks following the strength program play an important role in the training process. 
First of all, the load on the muscles of the throwing arm must be excluded during the first 
week. Then the power of throwing should be increased gradually. As a rule, 2-3 weeks is 
enough for the restoration of the feeling of throwing.
Conclusions
1. 
In many countries I was able to see that young athletes were using the depth jump from 
great heights and with high volume. This is not correct. It is very injurious.
2. 
The particular virtue of the shock method is its capability for significantly influencing the 
training effect on man's neuromuscular system. Therefore, this method should be used only 
by experienced top level athletes. As for young athletes, there are many other effective ex­
ercises that they should use.
3. 
It is necessary to emphasize that it is impossible, in any circumstance, to overrate the poten­
tial of the shock method.

SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
The shock method is only one of the many ways of special strength training and is not meant to 
replace the other ones.
The shock method should assume a definite place in the training system. This is determined by a 
full evaluation of the athlete's preparation and timed to coincide specifically with a definite stage 
of the yearly training cycle. The motor specifics of the particular sport, the objective of the train­
ing, the level of athlete's preparedness and competition calendar must all be taken into account.

######## framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology.md
---

# The Shock Method (Original Russian "Udarnyi Metod"), and Why "Plyometrics" Is a Loose Translation

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky developed the "shock method" (udarnyi metod) as a special
speed-strength training method exploiting connective and elastic tissue's ability to
store and release elastic energy during stretch-shortening of the muscle complex (running,
jumping, throwing, rapid lifting). The rise in concentric strength after rapid "shock"
loading comes from two sources: increased muscle tension from the myotatic (stretch)
reflex, and explosive release of elastic energy stored in connective/elastic tissue during
the eccentric phase. Historically, "pliometric" "was apparently coined to mean eccentric
contraction"; in this scheme of nomenclature (the text does not state it to be
specifically Russian), isometric retained its meaning of static contraction, miometric
meant concentric contraction, and pliometric meant eccentric contraction (printed 34); the
term "plyometrics," as adopted in the West, has drifted to describe a broader category of
jumping drills, many of which do not reproduce true shock-method characteristics. The
text's precise redefinition: the term plyometrics should refer to "an eccentric muscle
contraction ... suddenly terminated in an explosive isometric contraction, thereby
producing a powerful myotatic reflex, a sharp extension of the passive components of the
muscle complex and a subsequent explosive concentric contraction," and "should not refer
to ordinary jumping" (printed 34-35). (PDF pp. 45-46, printed pp. 34-35.)

**Why it works** — Inference: the stretch-shortening cycle mechanism (reflex potentiation
plus elastic energy return) is documented in modern SSC/plyometric research independent of
this text (e.g. Komi 2000, "Stretch-shortening cycle: a powerful model to study normal and
fatigued muscle," J Biomech 33:1197-1206); this entry's contribution is the terminology
history and the precise mechanical definition, which distinguishes genuine shock-method
work from ordinary jumping drills marketed under the same name.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful when auditing whether a program's "plyometric"
exercises actually meet the text's precise definition (a sudden eccentric-to-isometric-
to-concentric sequence) versus being ordinary jump training relabeled; this matters for
predicting whether the intended reactive-strength adaptation is actually being trained.
This library already traces Verkhoshansky's shock-method lineage at a higher level in
[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas|The
Soviet Lineage Behind Modern Sprint-Training Ideas]]; that entry credits him with "shock
method (plyometrics)" but does not cover the terminology history or mechanism given here,
so this entry adds a genuinely new angle rather than duplicating it.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** do not assume every drill called "plyometric" in
current commercial or popular usage (e.g. step-aerobics-style jumping) reproduces the
shock-method mechanism. "Russian scientists prefer to retain the term 'shock method' ...
and 'depth jumps'" (printed 34), while Siff separately proposes "powermetrics" for the
whole collection of jumping and rebound methods (Siff, 1998, printed 35). This terminology
distinction does not itself tell a coach which drills are safe or appropriate for a given
athlete; that is a separate training-age and readiness question.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach programming "plyometrics" for a novice athlete should
check whether the intended exercise involves a true rapid eccentric-to-concentric shock
transition (a depth jump) or is really just a submaximal hop/jump drill; the two carry very
different neuromuscular demands despite sharing the popular label.

# Depth Jumps: Once or Twice a Week, Kept 3-4 Days From Technique Sessions, Every 10-14 Days In Season and Not Within 10 Days of Competition

**What it is** — From the authors' depth-jump recommendations (PDF pp. 286-287 / printed pp. 275-276, verified against the page images):
- **Weekly frequency (item 3):** depth jumps "in the volume indicated should be done once or twice a week in training sessions devoted to special strength training", which can also include "localised exercises for other muscle groups and general developmental exercises executed with a small volume." But "Well-conditioned athletes can execute depth-jumps 3 times per week for 2 sets of 10 jumps at the completion of technical training in the particular sport."
- **Spacing from technique (item 4):** "Depth-jumps strongly excite the nervous system. Therefore, they should be used not less than 3-4 days before a technique training session. Sessions devoted to general physical preparation with a small volume of work should be done after depth-jump workouts."
- **Season (item 5):** "Depth-jumps occupy a fundamental place in the second half of the preparatory period of the yearly cycle. However, they can function as a means of maintaining the achieved level of special strength fitness in the competition period. During the competition period they should be included once every 10-14 days, but no later than 10 days before a competition."
- **Delayed effect (item 15):** integration "depends on not disrupting the delayed training effect of prior strength work. It should be noted that the use of depth-jumps as a means of stimulation can delay this effect for 5-6 days."

**Internal conflict, recorded:** item 4 keeps depth jumps at least 3-4 days before a technique session, while item 3 allows well-conditioned athletes three depth-jump sessions a week placed "at the completion of technical training." Three sessions a week tied to technical training cannot all sit 3-4 days before the next technique session. Both are on PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275; the book does not reconcile them.

**Why it works** — The authors' stated reasons: strong excitation of the nervous system (item 4) and a 5-6 day delay of the training effect of prior strength work (item 15). Neither cites a study. Inference: the in-season 10-day cut-off before competition is consistent with item 15's 5-6 day delayed effect plus a margin; the book does not make that link.

**When to apply** — Placing depth jumps in a football week or year. Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume"" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: the authors' in-season rule (one exposure every 10-14 days, none in the 10 days before a game) is far sparser than a weekly game schedule allows; read literally, a team playing every 7 days would have no legal in-season depth-jump day. That is a reason to treat the 10-day rule as written for track-and-field competition calendars, which the book does not say.

**When NOT to apply** — These are experience-based rules with no population, drop height or study given. They are written for an annual cycle with a long preparatory period and spaced competitions (the authors' examples elsewhere in 5.2.4 are track-and-field jumpers). Do not quote the 3-4 day spacing without the item 3 exception. The 5-6 day delay applies to depth jumps used "as a means of stimulation"; the book does not say how it scales with volume.

**Example** — The authors' own: depth jumps central in the second half of the preparatory period, then once every 10-14 days in the competition period, last one at least 10 days out (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275).

**Related** — [[heuristic--maximal-plyometric-and-depth-jump-volume-and-rest]]; [[claim--delayed-strength-training-effect-lag-before-gains-appear]] (Ch4.1, the delayed training effect); [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]]; [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]

# Depth-Jump and Maximal-Plyometric Volume and Rest: The Book Gives Two Incompatible Dosing Models

**What it is** — Section 5.2.4 gives the following dosing statements. They do not agree, so all are listed with locators.

**Model 1: maximal plyometrics dosed like a maximal lift.** The first, third and fourth statements are Siff's text (the powermetrics and 1RM-analogy passages; the section uses his term "powermetrics", PDF p. 279 / printed p. 268); prescription item 6 is from the authors' prescription list.
- "*Maximal plyometrics* essentially are low-repetition activities ... Just like maximal strength training with weights, these powerful impulses are not meant to be imposed on the musculature every workout, nor are multiple repetitions even possible or advisable. Moreover, a rest interval of 2-4 minutes is recommended between successive repetitions and as much as 10-12 minutes between sets" (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272, verified against the page image).
- Prescription item 6: "The rest interval between sets of maximal plyometric exercises should be about 10 minutes for power development (strength-speed and speed-strength) and much shorter intervals with submaximal plyometrics to develop explosive-strength endurance" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, verified against the page image).
- "several books advocate sessions with over 100 repetitions of plyometric movements ... This volume of *maximal plyometrics* (unlike sub-maximal plyometrics) is neither productive nor safe for any athlete. Maximal plyometrics, like maximal weight lifting, involves single all-out repetitions separated by a few minutes of rest" (PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282, verified against the page image).
- "classical plyometrics are 1 RM movements which require as much as several minutes of rest before recovery is complete" (PDF p. 294 / printed p. 283, text layer).

**Model 2: depth jumps in sets of 5-10.** Prescription item 4 is from the authors' prescription list (PDF p. 285); items 2 and 3 are from the depth-jump recommendations credited to "prolific experience" (PDF p. 286), a list whose figures (Figs 5.10, 5.11) are credited to Verkhoshansky (1977); the list itself carries no citation.
- Prescription item 4: "As an initial guideline, the dosage of plyometric exercises should not exceed 5-8 repetitions in one set" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, verified against the page image).
- Depth-jump item 2: "The optimal dosage of depth-jumps with an energetic vertical take-off in one training session should not exceed 4 sets of 10 jumps for well-conditioned athletes and 2-3 sets of 5-8 jumps for lesser conditioned athletes. Easy running and relaxation exercises for a period of 10-15 minutes should be done between sets" (same page, verified against the page image).
- Depth-jump item 3: "Well-conditioned athletes can execute depth-jumps 3 times per week for 2 sets of 10 jumps at the completion of technical training" (same page, verified against the page image).

**Depth-jump item 1, kept out of Model 2:** "Good results are obtained with depth-jumps using a complex of vertical jumps (Fig 5.11). Each exercise is executed in sets of 10 repetitions, with 1-15 minutes of rest between sets" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275; the page image prints "1-15", recorded as printed). Fig 5.11, "Jumping exercises for developing reactive ability (Verkhoshansky, 1977)" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, verified against the page image), shows ground-based vertical, tuck and split jumps with no box. Inference: "each exercise" most plausibly refers to that complex of ground jumps, so the sets of 10 and "1-15 minutes" are not a depth-jump dose.

**The conflict.** Model 1 says multiple repetitions of maximal plyometrics are not "possible or advisable" and separates single reps by 2-4 minutes. Model 2 prescribes sets of 10 energetic depth jumps, up to 40 per session, with rest given only between sets. Inference: Model 2 might be read as submaximal work, but depth-jump item 2 specifies "an energetic vertical take-off", and the 0.75-1.15 m heights in Ch4 are for advanced jumpers. Rest between sets of maximal or depth-jump work also varies: about 10 min (p. 274), 10-12 min (p. 272) and 10-15 min of easy running (p. 275). The book does not reconcile them.

**Why it works** — Model 1's stated reasons: maximal plyometrics are "extremely demanding on the central nervous system" and impose "great mechanical strain on the tendons, in particular" (PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282). Model 2's stated basis is "prolific experience with depth-jumps for developing jumping power" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275). Neither gives fatigue or recovery data.

**When to apply** — Inference: one way to use both is to treat Model 1 as the rule for truly maximal efforts (maximal height, rebound to a marker, near-maximal tension) and Model 2 as an upper volume cap for depth-jump sessions, keeping per-session counts at or under 2-3 × 5-8 for less-conditioned athletes and 4 × 10 for well-conditioned ones. The book does not make this split. For any athlete, the authors' quality rule holds: "It is the quality of the plyometric exercises, not the quantity, which is important" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 11). Eric's baseline: in-season "the stated rule is 'maintain intensity, reduce volume' rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Eric's baseline: "lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game" (line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)). Inference: Model 1's low-rep, long-rest structure fits the line-105 rule more directly than Model 2's sets of 10, and any maximal depth-jump session in season falls before that 72-hour cut-off.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not cite "4 × 10 depth jumps" as Supertraining's recommendation without the Model 1 statements beside it, or the reverse. "1-15 minutes" may be a misprint (Inference: 1.5 or 10-15 are possible readings), but the page prints 1-15, so do not quote a corrected value. None of these numbers comes with a cited study, population or drop height (except the Ch4 heights for advanced jumpers). The "over 100 repetitions" warning targets maximal plyometrics; the authors say submaximal plyometrics differ.

**Example** — The authors' own figures: lesser-conditioned athletes 2-3 sets of 5-8 energetic depth jumps with 10-15 minutes of easy running between sets (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275), against maximal rebounds as single reps 2-4 minutes apart with 10-12 minutes between sets (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272).

**Related** — [[heuristic--depth-jump-weekly-frequency-and-seasonal-placement]]; [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]; [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[claim--high-volume-plyometrics-do-not-build-rebound-fatigue-resistance]]; [[framework--resistance-training-prescription-by-goal]]

Easy running and relaxation exercises for a period of 10-15 minutes should be done between sets" (same page, verified against the page image).
- Depth-jump item 3: "Well-conditioned athletes can execute depth-jumps 3 times per week for 2 sets of 10 jumps at the completion of technical training" (same page, verified against the page image).

**Depth-jump item 1, kept out of Model 2:** "Good results are obtained with depth-jumps using a complex of vertical jumps (Fig 5.11). Each exercise is executed in sets of 10 repetitions, with 1-15 minutes of rest between sets" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275; the page image prints "1-15", recorded as printed). Fig 5.11, "Jumping exercises for developing reactive ability (Verkhoshansky, 1977)" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, verified against the page image), shows ground-based vertical, tuck and split jumps with no box. Inference: "each exercise" most plausibly refers to that complex of ground jumps, so the sets of 10 and "1-15 minutes" are not a depth-jump dose.

**The conflict.** Model 1 says multiple repetitions of maximal plyometrics are not "possible or advisable" and separates single reps by 2-4 minutes. Model 2 prescribes sets of 10 energetic depth jumps, up to 40 per session, with rest given only between sets. Inference: Model 2 might be read as submaximal work, but depth-jump item 2 specifies "an energetic vertical take-off", and the 0.75-1.15 m heights in Ch4 are for advanced jumpers. Rest between sets of maximal or depth-jump work also varies: about 10 min (p. 274), 10-12 min (p. 272) and 10-15 min of easy running (p. 275). The book does not reconcile them.

**Why it works** — Model 1's stated reasons: maximal plyometrics are "extremely demanding on the central nervous system" and impose "great mechanical strain on the tendons, in particular" (PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282). Model 2's stated basis is "prolific experience with depth-jumps for developing jumping power" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275). Neither gives fatigue or recovery data.

**When to apply** — Inference: one way to use both is to treat Model 1 as the rule for truly maximal efforts (maximal height, rebound to a marker, near-maximal tension) and Model 2 as an upper volume cap for depth-jump sessions, keeping per-session counts at or under 2-3 × 5-8 for less-conditioned athletes and 4 × 10 for well-conditioned ones. The book does not make this split. For any athlete, the authors' quality rule holds: "It is the quality of the plyometric exercises, not the quantity, which is important" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 11). Eric's baseline: in-season "the stated rule is 'maintain intensity, reduce volume' rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Eric's baseline: "lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game" (line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)). Inference: Model 1's low-rep, long-rest structure fits the line-105 rule more directly than Model 2's sets of 10, and any maximal depth-jump session in season falls before that 72-hour cut-off.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not cite "4 × 10 depth jumps" as Supertraining's recommendation without the Model 1 statements beside it, or the reverse. "1-15 minutes" may be a misprint (Inference: 1.5 or 10-15 are possible readings), but the page prints 1-15, so do not quote a corrected value. None of these numbers comes with a cited study, population or drop height (except the Ch4 heights for advanced jumpers). The "over 100 repetitions" warning targets maximal plyometrics; the authors say submaximal plyometrics differ.

**Example** — The authors' own figures: lesser-conditioned athletes 2-3 sets of 5-8 energetic depth jumps with 10-15 minutes of easy running between sets (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275), against maximal rebounds as single reps 2-4 minutes apart with 10-12 minutes between sets (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272).

# Before Depth Jumps: Months of Barbell, Jumping, Sprint and Skipping Work, Eccentric and Explosive-Isometric Strength, Static-Start Jumps, Then Low Hops

**What it is** — The authors' preparation rules (pages verified against the page images):
- "Depth-jumps require special preliminary preparation such as a significant volume of barbell exercises and traditional jumping, short sprints and skipping over a period of several months" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, item 1). Contra-indications: "Muscle or tendon fatigue, pain or soreness, as well as incompletely healed injuries" (same item).
- "depth-jumping is not a basic type of training to be indulged in lightly by athletes who are relatively unused to explosive or strongly resisted movements. For anyone who is not accustomed to movements such as weightlifting cleans, jerks, squats or hurdling, it is highly advisable that a preparatory programme using submaximal plyometrics, non-impact and non-plyometrics be followed" first (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276).
- **Eccentric and explosive-isometric strength first:** "a primary requirement for anyone contemplating the use of classical plyometrics is a high level of eccentric strength and explosive isometric strength. Herein lies the value of small-range squats, power cleans, power snatches, cleans from the hang, snatches from the hang, push presses or jerks, push presses or jerks from racks, and the descent of flights of stairs." Front and back squats both, "since they each model different types of jump (directly upwards versus forwards and upwards)." "Slow quasi-isometric squats over a moderate range with heavy weights should later lead to more rapid dips over a shallower range with lighter weights" (PDF pp. 287-288 / printed pp. 276-277).
- **Static start before dynamic start:** "it is initially useful to improve jumping ability from a static start, without exposing oneself to the greater musculotendinous stress of a dynamic start": standing broad and vertical jumps without a dip, then the vertical jump test "progressing from a static flexed knee start to a dynamic dip start with arms flung vigorously upwards" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277). Progress can be tracked with the Lewis formula ([[claim--lewis-formula-estimates-jump-power-from-bodymass-and-height]]).
- **Low hops:** "hopping on the spot at a frequency which feels most comfortable for the athlete, using a few sets of about 25 repetitions", then small forward, backward, sideward, forward-backward and zig-zag hops, then vertical hops "as rapidly as possible, again using a few sets of about 20 repetitions" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, item 6). Rope skipping is useful, but "long periods of skipping are not the appropriate form of preparatory drill" because the aim is speed-strength, not endurance (item 7).
- **Technique and complexity:** learn normal jumping first, with "the correct lumbar-pelvic rhythm, as is also used during clean pulls or power cleans from the ground" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 13). "Great caution" with depth jumps involving "one-legged thrusts, changes of direction or complex variations, since the injury risk is significantly higher" (item 14).
- Then integrate: "As eccentric, isometric and concentric strength increases ... the athlete may progress to actions which more rapidly integrate all three aspects of plyometric movement"; the same principles apply to upper-body work (medicine ball catching and throwing, plyometric press-ups and bench presses) (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277).

**Why it works** — The authors derive the preparation from the action itself: because plyometric actions involve "a powerful eccentric amortisation phase terminating in an explosive isometric contraction", eccentric and explosive-isometric strength come first; because the concentric phase is reflex-assisted, static-start jumping builds the concentric part "without exposing oneself to the greater musculotendinous stress of a dynamic start" (PDF pp. 287-288 / printed pp. 276-277).

**When to apply** — Freshmen, return-to-training athletes, or anyone without a lifting and jumping base. Eric's baseline: the Vermeil hierarchy (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, "each level a required foundation for the next") is the department's programming "compass" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 101). Inference: the authors' sequence (strength base, static jumps, low hops, then depth jumps) is the same ordering applied inside the power level. Inference: single-leg and change-of-direction depth jumps, the most football-like variants, are the ones the authors flag as highest risk, so they come last.

**When NOT to apply** — "Several months" is not quantified, and no strength threshold is given here (for the 1.5-2 × bodymass squat rule, see [[claim--squat-1-5-to-2-bodymass-rule-applies-to-maximal-depth-jumps-only]]). Inference: athletes with a long sporting history of running, jumping and lifting may already meet much of this preparation; the authors also say an athlete's sport may already supply most plyometric loading ([[claim--plyometric-injury-risk-comes-from-prescription-not-the-method]]).

**Example** — The authors' own: hopping on the spot in a few sets of about 25, moving to multi-directional hops, then fast vertical hops in sets of about 20 (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275).

# Depth-Jump Execution Cues: Step Off Relaxed, Land on the Balls of the Feet With Shallow Amortisation, Eyes Up, Breath Held Through Contact

**What it is** — The authors' execution rules for depth jumps and plyometric drills (pages verified against the page images unless marked):
- **Leaving the box:** "Depth-jumping necessitates falling in a relaxed state, but not jumping, off the box" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 10).
- **Landing:** "land with the legs slightly flexed, muscles mildly tensed and on the balls of the feet in order to avoid an excessive shock. The depth of amortisation should not be great and the subsequent take-off needs to be executed very quickly with an energetic throwing upwards of the arms" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275).
- **Target:** "strive with the hands or head to reach some height indicated by some marker if the take-off is executed upward, or to land at some point if it is directed upward and forward"; a gain in height or distance "clearly indicates improvement in special fitness, which always has a positive effect on the athlete's emotional state" (same page).
- **Starting posture:** the amortisation "should be of minimal duration, but sufficient to create impulsive contraction of the muscles. Therefore, the initial posture with respect to the joint angles should correspond to the same position in which the working movement begins in the sporting exercise" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 2).
- **Range of motion** in the Fig 5.9 resistance-apparatus exercises "should be somewhat greater than the required coordination range of the exercise in order to enhance shock absorption by the soft tissues and thereby avoid impact injury" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274).
- **Head and gaze:** "Flexing the head downward to look at the floor before take-off may result in spurious muscle contraction or altered timing. Similarly if the head is not thrust upwards during the take-off, maximal height will not be reached" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 9).
- **Warm-up:** plyometric training "should be preceded by a good warmup of the intensively involved muscles" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 3).
- **Breathing:** "It is vital that the athlete holds the breath during the amortisation and early propulsion phase to stabilise the body, offer pneumatic shock absorption and to increase the rebound force. Forced exhalation may accompany the remainder of the propulsion phase" (PDF p. 284 / printed p. 273). Item 12: "the breath should be held and never released during the contact phase or any phase where maximal effort is to be produced. Exhalation during any landing phase reduces overall stability and increases the loading on the spine during depth-jumping" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276).

**Why it works** — Reasons given by the authors are in the quotes: avoiding excessive shock (landing posture), stability and "pneumatic shock absorption" (breath), timing (gaze), and shock absorption by soft tissues (range). They cite no study for these cues.

**When to apply** — Coaching any depth-jump or rebound session; the cues are concrete and observable. Inference: the starting-posture rule (item 2) gives a way to make a depth jump more specific to a football stance or a block-start angle by matching the landing knee and hip angle to the sport's start position.

**When NOT to apply** — The two breathing statements differ in detail: p. 273 allows "forced exhalation" during the remainder of the propulsion phase, which is still ground contact in a rebound, while item 12 says the breath is "never released during the contact phase." Inference: read together, the cautious reading is breath held through landing and early push-off. Item 2's "minimal duration but sufficient" depth and the Fig 5.9 "somewhat greater" range are not quantified. Inference: maximal breath-holding effort raises blood pressure; the book does not discuss this for athletes with cardiovascular conditions.

**Example** — The authors' own: jumping up to touch a marker with the hands or head after the depth jump (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275).

######## heuristic--depth-jump-height-set-by-transition-speed-and-heel-contact.md
# Set Depth-Jump Height by Strength Fitness: Too High Once the Transition Slows or the Heels Are Driven to the Ground; Raise Speed Before Height

**What it is** — The authors' rules for choosing drop height in training (all on pages verified against the page image):
- "The optimal depth of the jump is determined by the athlete's strength fitness, while the athlete should ensure that significant dynamic force is developed without slowing down the transition from eccentric to concentric work by the muscles involved" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274).
- "The optimal height of a depth jump does not result in a landing where the heel is forced to the ground by momentum" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 8).
- "One should aim to increase the speed and acceleration of movement before increasing the drop height or take-off height" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 5).
- "One should begin at a relatively low height and increase it gradually to the optimal height. It makes sense to begin by jumping upward and forward and only after sufficient training, to jump strictly upward" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, item 1).
- Height is preferred over added weight, and a force plate can find the height for a required force (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 1).
- For jumping power "one can work without an additional load and utilise only falling bodymass" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274). Fig 5.10 (Verkhoshansky, 1977) shows three variants: two under "Horizontal Projection" (after the drop, the athlete rebounds forward over low objects drawn on the ground) and one under "Vertical Projection" (rebound upward toward a hanging marker) (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, read from the image; the drawings are small, so the object details are approximate).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the transition: height is only useful while it raises dynamic force without "slowing down the transition from eccentric to concentric work". Heels forced to the ground is their visible sign that momentum has overwhelmed the athlete. Inference: a heel strike means the ankle has been driven through its range, which lengthens the amortisation the authors want kept short; the book states only the rule.

**When to apply** — Inference: with a force plate or contact mat, find each athlete's height by stepping the box up until contact time rises or rebound height falls, and stop below that point; on the field, watch for heels hitting the ground. This individual approach is consistent with the authors' "determined by the athlete's strength fitness." Eric's baseline: mRSI from daily CMJ testing "was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 74, Explicit). Inference: a drop-jump RSI (jump height over contact time) at stepped heights would be a separate test of the authors' "without slowing down the transition" rule; the baseline has no drop-jump test.

**When NOT to apply** — The Ch4.2.3 figures put the optimum for advanced jumpers at 0.75-1.15 m ([[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]); the rules here give no number, and the authors stress "using considerably lower jump heights with anyone who is unused to this type of training" (Ch4.2.3, PDF p. 233 / printed p. 222, verified against the page image). The heel rule is a coaching sign, not a measured threshold. Upward-and-forward before strictly upward is the authors' order; they give no reason.

**Example** — The authors' own: the three Fig 5.10 depth-jump variants, and the progression from upward-and-forward to strictly upward jumps (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275).

**Related** — [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]; [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]]; [[heuristic--rate-plyometric-intensity-by-contact-momentum-from-drop-height]]; [[heuristic--depth-jump-execution-cues-landing-gaze-breath]]; [[heuristic--match-plyometric-prescription-to-joint-angle-and-fiber-type]]
######## claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force.md
# The Optimal Depth-Jump Drop Height Is 0.75-1.15 Metres: Maximal Power at the Low End, Maximal Force at the High End

**What it is** — Fig 4.7 (PDF p. 232, printed p. 221; Verkhoshansky, 1977) plots force, in
bodyweights, against time for three vertical jumps: (1) jumping from rest from a low squat,
(2) the usual jump with a dip or amortisation phase, (3) a jump after a depth jump from
0.4 m. The caption gives jump heights of 0.67 m, 0.74 m and 0.80 m respectively. Verified
against the page image (readings from the figure, approximate): curve 1 peaks early, about
1.4-1.5 BW at about 0.08-0.1 s, and ends about 0.3 s; curve 2 first drops below bodyweight
(about 0.6 BW at about 0.15 s), then peaks about 1.4 BW at about 0.5 s and ends about 0.8 s;
curve 3 peaks about 3 BW at about 0.1 s and ends about 0.25 s. Curves 1 and 2 have similar
peaks, and curve 2's is the later; only curve 3 is clearly higher and earlier.

Depth jumps from a range of drop heights (Fig 4.10, PDF p. 234, printed p. 223): the text
states that "maximal force (Fmax) increases up to a height of 1.15 metres, then diminishes
sharply, while movement time begins by changing insignificantly, then increasing sharply.
Maximum power and reactivity are achieved using a drop height of approximately 0.75 metres"
(PDF p. 233, printed p. 222). Verified against the page image (approximate): Fmax peaks near
1.1-1.15 m and falls sharply to 1.55 m; the figure also carries a Power curve, not named in
the caption, peaking about 0.75 m; RC peaks about 0.8 m; ground contact time t dips slightly
to a minimum about 0.75 m, then rises sharply. The authors conclude that the optimal range of
depth jumping for stimulating muscular activity is 0.75-1.15 metres, "because at the lower
end of this range the muscles are working at maximal power and at the upper end they are
working at maximal dynamic force". This finding "forms the basis for the recommendations for
using depth jumps in the training of advanced jumpers (Verkhoshansky 1963, 1964, 1966)",
though it is "preferable to err on the conservative side of using considerably lower jump
heights with anyone who is unused to this type of training and to strictly limit the volume
of this type of 'shock' training" (p.222).

The book states the result past 1.15 m two ways. The Fig 4.10 text says Fmax "diminishes
sharply" past 1.15 m; the next paragraph says further increases in height "significantly
decrease the magnitude of the dynamic parameters of the take-off", support time increases
quickly because the eccentric-concentric switch is lengthened, and "the maximum dynamic force
of take-off and the speed of muscular contraction stabilise and do not increase any further"
(p.222). The figure shows a sharp fall. Both are recorded. The contradiction concerns only what
happens past the optimum; both readings agree force does not rise past 1.15 m, so it does
not dispute the entry's claim (optimal range 0.75-1.15 m), and confidence is `supported`. The take-off comprises amortisation (kinetic energy of the fall
absorbed, with increasing depth of knee flexion) and the thrust proper (fairly constant
speed of muscle contraction) (p.222).

Loaded depth jumps (Fig 4.9, PDF p. 234, printed p. 223; the caption is on the page image, not
in the text layer): after an unloaded depth jump (M = mass of athlete) and with an extra 10,
20, 30 and 40 kg. Verified against the page image: rebound height h2, force F and RC fall and
contact time t rises as load increases from M to M+40 kg. The text groups Figs 4.9 and 4.10
as showing the same tendency as the thrown-load experiment "under other conditions, although
these have their own peculiarities", and concludes "it is not beneficial to increase kinetic
energy by use of heavier loads" (p.222; see
[[claim--thrown-load-height-decreases-with-load-increases-with-drop-height]]). (PDF pp.
232-234, printed pp. 221-223, "4.2.3 Kinetic Energy and Strength Processes," Figs 4.7, 4.9,
4.10.)

**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is elastic-energy storage during
amortisation and its release in the thrust (see
[[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]]), and for heights
past the optimum the lengthened switch from eccentric to concentric work (p.222). Inference:
at greater drop heights more of the force capacity may go to braking, which would fit force
rising to 1.15 m while power and reactivity peak earlier; the book does not state this.

**When to apply** — For advanced jumpers (Verkhoshansky 1963, 1964, 1966; p.222), use about
0.75 m when the training goal is maximal power and reactivity, and up to about 1.15 m when
the goal is maximal dynamic force, per this protocol. For athletes unused to depth-jump
training, start considerably lower and strictly limit volume, per the authors' caution.
Inference: this gives a citable historical anchor for programming depth-jump height, distinct
from the fixed 0.4 m depth-jump reactivity test already in this library (see
[[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]]).

**When NOT to apply** — This is single-lab, era-specific data (Verkhoshansky, 1963-1977) on
an unspecified population (the authors do not state training age, sport or sample size for
the drop-height experiment); do not apply 0.75 m and 1.15 m to every athlete without
accounting for the factors the authors name: whether the athlete is used to this training,
bodymass, additional load and fall height (p.222). Do
not cite the book as saying force merely plateaus past 1.15 m, or merely falls: it says both
(p.222). Do not conflate this variable drop-height range with the fixed 0.4 m reactivity test
(see Related).

**Example** — The book's own example is the Fig 4.7, 4.9 and 4.10 data described above; no
further example is added here.

**Related** — [[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]],
[[claim--thrown-load-height-decreases-with-load-increases-with-drop-height]],
[[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]] (Ch3.2.1, a related but distinct
fixed 0.4 m depth-jump protocol measuring reactive ability rather than optimal training drop
height),
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]; [[heuristic--depth-jump-height-set-by-transition-speed-and-heel-contact]] (5.2.4, drop height set by an unslowed eccentric-concentric transition and no forced heel contact, with no number given; it cites this entry's 0.75-1.15 m range for advanced jumpers); [[heuristic--rate-plyometric-intensity-by-contact-momentum-from-drop-height]] (5.2.4, Siff's intensity scale by momentum at contact from drop height; it cites this entry's range as the upper limit past which the transition slows)

######## heuristic--depth-jump-height-set-by-transition-speed-and-heel-contact.md
# Set Depth-Jump Height by Strength Fitness: Too High Once the Transition Slows or the Heels Are Driven to the Ground; Raise Speed Before Height

**What it is** — The authors' rules for choosing drop height in training (all on pages verified against the page image):
- "The optimal depth of the jump is determined by the athlete's strength fitness, while the athlete should ensure that significant dynamic force is developed without slowing down the transition from eccentric to concentric work by the muscles involved" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274).
- "The optimal height of a depth jump does not result in a landing where the heel is forced to the ground by momentum" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 8).
- "One should aim to increase the speed and acceleration of movement before increasing the drop height or take-off height" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 5).
- "One should begin at a relatively low height and increase it gradually to the optimal height. It makes sense to begin by jumping upward and forward and only after sufficient training, to jump strictly upward" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, item 1).
- Height is preferred over added weight, and a force plate can find the height for a required force (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 1).
- For jumping power "one can work without an additional load and utilise only falling bodymass" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274). Fig 5.10 (Verkhoshansky, 1977) shows three variants: two under "Horizontal Projection" (after the drop, the athlete rebounds forward over low objects drawn on the ground) and one under "Vertical Projection" (rebound upward toward a hanging marker) (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, read from the image; the drawings are small, so the object details are approximate).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the transition: height is only useful while it raises dynamic force without "slowing down the transition from eccentric to concentric work". Heels forced to the ground is their visible sign that momentum has overwhelmed the athlete. Inference: a heel strike means the ankle has been driven through its range, which lengthens the amortisation the authors want kept short; the book states only the rule.

**When to apply** — Inference: with a force plate or contact mat, find each athlete's height by stepping the box up until contact time rises or rebound height falls, and stop below that point; on the field, watch for heels hitting the ground. This individual approach is consistent with the authors' "determined by the athlete's strength fitness." Eric's baseline: mRSI from daily CMJ testing "was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 74, Explicit). Inference: a drop-jump RSI (jump height over contact time) at stepped heights would be a separate test of the authors' "without slowing down the transition" rule; the baseline has no drop-jump test.

**When NOT to apply** — The Ch4.2.3 figures put the optimum for advanced jumpers at 0.75-1.15 m ([[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]); the rules here give no number, and the authors stress "using considerably lower jump heights with anyone who is unused to this type of training" (Ch4.2.3, PDF p. 233 / printed p. 222, verified against the page image). The heel rule is a coaching sign, not a measured threshold. Upward-and-forward before strictly upward is the authors' order; they give no reason.

**Example** — The authors' own: the three Fig 5.10 depth-jump variants, and the progression from upward-and-forward to strictly upward jumps (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275).

**Related** — [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]; [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]]; [[heuristic--rate-plyometric-intensity-by-contact-momentum-from-drop-height]]; [[heuristic--depth-jump-execution-cues-landing-gaze-breath]]; [[heuristic--match-plyometric-prescription-to-joint-angle-and-fiber-type]]
######## claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force.md
# The Optimal Depth-Jump Drop Height Is 0.75-1.15 Metres: Maximal Power at the Low End, Maximal Force at the High End

**What it is** — Fig 4.7 (PDF p. 232, printed p. 221; Verkhoshansky, 1977) plots force, in
bodyweights, against time for three vertical jumps: (1) jumping from rest from a low squat,
(2) the usual jump with a dip or amortisation phase, (3) a jump after a depth jump from
0.4 m. The caption gives jump heights of 0.67 m, 0.74 m and 0.80 m respectively. Verified
against the page image (readings from the figure, approximate): curve 1 peaks early, about
1.4-1.5 BW at about 0.08-0.1 s, and ends about 0.3 s; curve 2 first drops below bodyweight
(about 0.6 BW at about 0.15 s), then peaks about 1.4 BW at about 0.5 s and ends about 0.8 s;
curve 3 peaks about 3 BW at about 0.1 s and ends about 0.25 s. Curves 1 and 2 have similar
peaks, and curve 2's is the later; only curve 3 is clearly higher and earlier.

Depth jumps from a range of drop heights (Fig 4.10, PDF p. 234, printed p. 223): the text
states that "maximal force (Fmax) increases up to a height of 1.15 metres, then diminishes
sharply, while movement time begins by changing insignificantly, then increasing sharply.
Maximum power and reactivity are achieved using a drop height of approximately 0.75 metres"
(PDF p. 233, printed p. 222). Verified against the page image (approximate): Fmax peaks near
1.1-1.15 m and falls sharply to 1.55 m; the figure also carries a Power curve, not named in
the caption, peaking about 0.75 m; RC peaks about 0.8 m; ground contact time t dips slightly
to a minimum about 0.75 m, then rises sharply. The authors conclude that the optimal range of
depth jumping for stimulating muscular activity is 0.75-1.15 metres, "because at the lower
end of this range the muscles are working at maximal power and at the upper end they are
working at maximal dynamic force". This finding "forms the basis for the recommendations for
using depth jumps in the training of advanced jumpers (Verkhoshansky 1963, 1964, 1966)",
though it is "preferable to err on the conservative side of using considerably lower jump
heights with anyone who is unused to this type of training and to strictly limit the volume
of this type of 'shock' training" (p.222).

The book states the result past 1.15 m two ways. The Fig 4.10 text says Fmax "diminishes
sharply" past 1.15 m; the next paragraph says further increases in height "significantly
decrease the magnitude of the dynamic parameters of the take-off", support time increases
quickly because the eccentric-concentric switch is lengthened, and "the maximum dynamic force
of take-off and the speed of muscular contraction stabilise and do not increase any further"
(p.222). The figure shows a sharp fall. Both are recorded. The contradiction concerns only what
happens past the optimum; both readings agree force does not rise past 1.15 m, so it does
not dispute the entry's claim (optimal range 0.75-1.15 m), and confidence is `supported`. The take-off comprises amortisation (kinetic energy of the fall
absorbed, with increasing depth of knee flexion) and the thrust proper (fairly constant
speed of muscle contraction) (p.222).

Loaded depth jumps (Fig 4.9, PDF p. 234, printed p. 223; the caption is on the page image, not
in the text layer): after an unloaded depth jump (M = mass of athlete) and with an extra 10,
20, 30 and 40 kg. Verified against the page image: rebound height h2, force F and RC fall and
contact time t rises as load increases from M to M+40 kg. The text groups Figs 4.9 and 4.10
as showing the same tendency as the thrown-load experiment "under other conditions, although
these have their own peculiarities", and concludes "it is not beneficial to increase kinetic
energy by use of heavier loads" (p.222; see
[[claim--thrown-load-height-decreases-with-load-increases-with-drop-height]]). (PDF pp.
232-234, printed pp. 221-223, "4.2.3 Kinetic Energy and Strength Processes," Figs 4.7, 4.9,
4.10.)

**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is elastic-energy storage during
amortisation and its release in the thrust (see
[[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]]), and for heights
past the optimum the lengthened switch from eccentric to concentric work (p.222). Inference:
at greater drop heights more of the force capacity may go to braking, which would fit force
rising to 1.15 m while power and reactivity peak earlier; the book does not state this.

**When to apply** — For advanced jumpers (Verkhoshansky 1963, 1964, 1966; p.222), use about
0.75 m when the training goal is maximal power and reactivity, and up to about 1.15 m when
the goal is maximal dynamic force, per this protocol. For athletes unused to depth-jump
training, start considerably lower and strictly limit volume, per the authors' caution.
Inference: this gives a citable historical anchor for programming depth-jump height, distinct
from the fixed 0.4 m depth-jump reactivity test already in this library (see
[[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]]).

**When NOT to apply** — This is single-lab, era-specific data (Verkhoshansky, 1963-1977) on
an unspecified population (the authors do not state training age, sport or sample size for
the drop-height experiment); do not apply 0.75 m and 1.15 m to every athlete without
accounting for the factors the authors name: whether the athlete is used to this training,
bodymass, additional load and fall height (p.222). Do
not cite the book as saying force merely plateaus past 1.15 m, or merely falls: it says both
(p.222). Do not conflate this variable drop-height range with the fixed 0.4 m reactivity test
(see Related).

**Example** — The book's own example is the Fig 4.7, 4.9 and 4.10 data described above; no
further example is added here.

**Related** — [[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]],
[[claim--thrown-load-height-decreases-with-load-increases-with-drop-height]],
[[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]] (Ch3.2.1, a related but distinct
fixed 0.4 m depth-jump protocol measuring reactive ability rather than optimal training drop
height),
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]; [[heuristic--depth-jump-height-set-by-transition-speed-and-heel-contact]] (5.2.4, drop height set by an unslowed eccentric-concentric transition and no forced heel contact, with no number given; it cites this entry's 0.75-1.15 m range for advanced jumpers); [[heuristic--rate-plyometric-intensity-by-contact-momentum-from-drop-height]] (5.2.4, Siff's intensity scale by momentum at contact from drop height; it cites this entry's range as the upper limit past which the transition slows)

# Interval Resistance Training (Extensive and Intensive) and Cluster Sets

**What it is** — The authors define interval resistance training by analogy with track: "the primary aim of interval training is generally to develop strength-endurance by means of systematically alternating work and recovery phases", with rest "(preferably active rest)" too short for full recovery "so that the athlete is forced to cope with increasing exhaustion" (PDF p. 409 / printed p. 398, checked against the page image). They split it into two broad categories, "one to increase strength or power and the other to increase endurance", and the endurance category into two methods (PDF p. 409):

| | Extensive interval | Intensive interval |
|---|---|---|
| Develops | "medium duration strength-endurance" and recovery capacity | "short-duration strength-endurance" and recovery capacity |
| Load | "30-40% of 1RM" | "50-60% of 1RM" |
| Sets x reps | "5-6 sets of 20-30 repetitions" | "3-6 sets, where each set is performed to failure" |
| Rest | "1-2 minutes" | "10-90 seconds", by exercise, load, fitness and loading duration |
| Energy | below 40% "arterial blood flow is not restricted" and "'aerobic' energy processes predominate" | higher loads "inhibit arterial blood flow and anaerobic energy processes predominate" |
| Heart rate | large muscle groups needed to reach the level "recommended for aerobic conditioning, e.g. 75% of (220-Age)" | "can readily increase heart rates to over 180 beats/min" |
| Circuits | "Specially designed circuit training programmes" can serve | special circuits with "1-3 minutes" between circuits |

For extensive work the authors want "the larger muscle groups such as the quadriceps, glutei, pectorals and erector spinae"; "bicep curls, calf raises and tricep push-downs play a minimal role in elevating the heart rate" (PDF p. 409).

**Cluster training** is "another form of interval training": one or more repetitions "with a 10-20 second interval between each repetition or cluster of repetitions in an extended set". "Characteristically, the minimum load used is one's 5RM and 4-6 sets are performed" (PDF p. 409 / printed p. 398). *Extensive clustering*: "4-6 repetitions with one's 4-6RM, with 10 second rest intervals between each cluster", or stripping-style with the load cut "by 10-20%" and a 10 s rest after each set (PDF pp. 409-410). *Intensive clustering*: "4-6 sets of only one repetition with 75-90% of 1RM, with about a 20 second rest between repetitions for 4-6 repetitions" (PDF p. 410 / printed p. 399, image). That last sentence is unclear as printed: it gives both "sets of only one repetition" and "4-6 repetitions" without saying how they nest.

**Why `contested`.** The rating applies only to the cluster-set loads; the extensive and intensive interval prescriptions are not in dispute. The same paragraph sets the minimum at "one's 5RM" (PDF p. 409) but prescribes extensive clustering "with one's 4-6RM" (a 6RM is lighter than a 5RM) and a stripping form that cuts the load "by 10-20%" after each set (PDF pp. 409-410), both of which can take the load below that minimum; intensive clustering then gives "75-90% of 1RM" (PDF p. 410). All of these state the load for the same method. Inference: the authors' own maximal pyramid puts 6 repetitions at 85% of 1RM, with values "derived from the equations associated with Fig 1.9" (PDF p. 409), so by the book's own figures a 5RM sits above 85%, and the lower end of the intensive range (75%) falls below the stated minimum. The book does not reconcile them.

A second internal conflict touches this section: the weightlifting method rests "1-5 minutes" between singles (PDF p. 406), while this section says weightlifting and powerlifting rely on near-maximal singles "with a few seconds of rest between repetitions" (PDF p. 409). The two passages may describe different methods (sets of singles against clustered singles), and the book does not say which; see [[framework--maximal-supramaximal-circa-maximal-and-submaximal-methods]].

**Different method, not a conflict.** Chapter 5's circuit guidelines give aerobic circuits "20-40" repetitions at "usually not more than 30% of 1RM" and anaerobic circuits "3-8" repetitions at "usually more than 70% of 1RM" ([[framework--aerobic-vs-anaerobic-circuit-parameters]], PDF p. 315 / printed p. 304). Those are station prescriptions for circuits; the figures here are for interval sets. # Interval Resistance Training (Extensive and Intensive) and Cluster Sets

**What it is** — The authors define interval resistance training by analogy with track: "the primary aim of interval training is generally to develop strength-endurance by means of systematically alternating work and recovery phases", with rest "(preferably active rest)" too short for full recovery "so that the athlete is forced to cope with increasing exhaustion" (PDF p. 409 / printed p. 398, checked against the page image). They split it into two broad categories, "one to increase strength or power and the other to increase endurance", and the endurance category into two methods (PDF p. 409):

| | Extensive interval | Intensive interval |
|---|---|---|
| Develops | "medium duration strength-endurance" and recovery capacity | "short-duration strength-endurance" and recovery capacity |
| Load | "30-40% of 1RM" | "50-60% of 1RM" |
| Sets x reps | "5-6 sets of 20-30 repetitions" | "3-6 sets, where each set is performed to failure" |
| Rest | "1-2 minutes" | "10-90 seconds", by exercise, load, fitness and loading duration |
| Energy | below 40% "arterial blood flow is not restricted" and "'aerobic' energy processes predominate" | higher loads "inhibit arterial blood flow and anaerobic energy processes predominate" |
| Heart rate | large muscle groups needed to reach the level "recommended for aerobic conditioning, e.g. 75% of (220-Age)" | "can readily increase heart rates to over 180 beats/min" |
| Circuits | "Specially designed circuit training programmes" can serve | special circuits with "1-3 minutes" between circuits |

# The Reactivity Coefficient (RC) and Verkhoshansky's Depth-Jump Reactivity Test

**What it is** — Reactive ability (the neuromuscular capacity to generate explosive force
via a preliminary stretch immediately before concentric work) is quantified with a
**Reactivity Coefficient**, which the text defines three ways without fully reconciling
them: earlier (2.2.1, printed 108) as "the explosive strength index relative to body
weight," RC = Fmax/(tmax.W) = RFDmax/W; here, the lab-only form RC = K2/K1 (a ratio of two
characteristics of muscular work, e.g. power, before and after the stretch), and the
field-practical form **RC = Fmax / (tmax x m x g)**, where Fmax is peak force, tmax is time
to reach it, m is the moving mass (or bodymass), and g is gravitational acceleration. Despite
that formula, the text separately states that in the reactivity test itself, "the
coefficient of reactivity was determined from the length of the support period and analysis
of the mean take-off force" (printed 137), not a literal Fmax/tmax calculation; the text
does not explain how the two are reconciled. Verkhoshansky's own "reactivity test" protocol:
a series of vertical jumps without arm-swing, performed after a depth-jump from 0.4 m,
unloaded and then with 10, 20, 30, and 40 kg added (fixed absolute loads, not expressed as a
percentage of the athlete's So); jump height and support-period duration are recorded and
plotted against added mass. Findings from this
protocol: reactive ability correlates with strength most strongly at large loads (R = 0.95
at 30-40 kg loads, weak at lighter loads); RC correlates more strongly with support-period
time than with force in every load condition; absolute strength has a *negative* effect on
contraction speed with small/no added load but a *positive* effect with large added load
(40 kg), while high *relative* strength has the opposite pattern (positive with light
loads, negative with heavy loads); and cross-sport testing (Fig 3.9-3.10) found jumpers
had the highest RC and middle-distance runners the lowest, with RC showing a strong linear
relationship (R ≈ 0.95) to triple-jump performance specifically. (PDF pp. 146-149, printed
pp. 135-138, "Quickness and Reactive Ability," Figs 3.7-3.10.)

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism: a preliminary stretch elastically deforms the
muscle-tendon complex, storing potential energy that converts to kinetic energy on the
subsequent contraction, adding to active muscular force. **Inference:** RC's specific
formula (force over time-to-peak times system mass) is not explained sentence-by-sentence
in the text beyond this general stretch-energy mechanism; the fact that it tracks support-period
time more tightly than raw force output is reported as an empirical correlation finding,
not derived from a stated causal mechanism.

**When to apply** — Use the RC formula's logic (peak force relative to time-to-peak and
system mass) as the conceptual ancestor of modern reactive strength index (RSI) metrics.
**Eric's baseline:** modified RSI (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is already the department's
chosen daily-readiness marker on ForceDecks (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
neuromuscular monitoring," citing `2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`). **Inference:** this
framework is a plausible historical/conceptual ancestor of that metric (RC = F/(t x m x g)
versus mRSI = jump height / time to take-off, not contact time); this lineage claim is not
stated in either source. The load-dependent strength-speed finding here
(absolute strength helps at heavy loads, hurts at light loads; relative strength does the
reverse) is a useful interpretive lens for reading an individual athlete's mRSI trend
alongside their absolute- and relative-strength testing numbers.

# Verkhoshansky: The Shock Method Is a Forced Shock Stretch of Tensed Muscle, a Different Entity From "Plyometrics", and He Is Not Its "Father"

**What it is** — Section 9.2 is a first-person paper by Verkhoshansky ("Dr. Yuri Verkhoshansky" under the heading, PDF 574 / p.563). He defines the method: "The regime, in which an external resistance is actively overcome after being preceded by a sharp preliminary stretch of the muscles, is most effective for training explosive strength (Verkhoshansky, 1960). This technique is called the Shock Method for development of explosive strength and reactive ability (Verkhoshansky, 1961)." He then says: "in USA the Shock Method is most often called *plyometrics*. This is not correct. The Shock Method and plyometric training are different entities" (PDF 574 / p.563). Under "I am not the father of plyometrics" he says being called "father of plyometrics" "gives me pleasure to hear this, but it is incorrect"; the term "to name my shock method, was invented by my friend, Fred Wilt", a former Olympic runner, NCAA champion and Purdue track coach, with whom he "corresponded ... in the 1960's" (PDF 575 / p.564). He warns that "plyometrics" "could be confused with the term 'pliometric'", the old anatomy term for the "yielding" regime in which "the external load on the muscles is much greater than the tension developed during the contraction, when the muscles are stretching" (footnote 23 cites Faulkner, 2003, J Appl Physiol 95: 455-459, and Faulkner et al., 1997, MSSE 29(5)). His defining feature: "The specific characteristic of my method is expressed in **the shock stretch of the muscle under tension**. This method has a compulsory (forced) character when the neuromuscular system is forced to display a high level of power against a significant external mechanical influence" (PDF 575 / p.564, bold on the page; all quotes checked against the page images).

**Why it works** — His stated reasoning: the shock stretch of strained muscle is "a high powered training influence for the neuromuscular system" because the system is forced, by an external mechanical impact, to produce high power (PDF 575 / p.564). The forcing comes from outside (the fall), not from the athlete's intent. Inference: this is why he separates it from "plyometric training": a jump the athlete starts voluntarily, with no imposed impact, lacks the "compulsory" element he names as the method's specific characteristic. He does not spell out which drills fall on which side.

**When to apply** — When a programme lists "plyometrics", use his test: is there an external impact that sharply stretches muscle already under tension (a depth jump, a drop catch), or only a self-started jump? Only the first is his shock method. This sharpens the 1.6 terminology entry ([[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]), which reports the authors' wider point that Western "plyometrics" drifted to cover ordinary jumping. Eric's baseline: "we incorporate the countermovement jump and the isometric mid-thigh pull to get a dynamic strength index, to determine whether we need more plyometric training or more max-strength training" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 76, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q21)). Inference: when DSI points to "more plyometric training", his distinction asks whether that means shock-method depth jumps or submaximal jumping, which carry different loads.

**When NOT to apply** — The history is his own account, with no source beyond the footnotes on Wilt's books (footnote 22, a bookfinder URL) and the Faulkner terminology papers. The publisher's back cover (PDF 590, not part of 9.2) calls him "the Russian researcher who invented plyometric training"; that is the publisher's wording, which his own text rejects. "Different entities" is asserted, not defined drill by drill, so do not use it to rule a specific drill in or out without the impact test above (Inference). The 1960 and 1961 dates are his self-citations; the 9.2 paper gives no bibliography for them.

**Example** — His own: the depth jump, where landing from a height imposes "a sharp preliminary stretch" on tensed leg extensors before the take-off (PDF 574-575 / pp.563-564).

**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] (1.6, the pliometric, miometric, isometric scheme and the authors' precise definition); [[case-study--half-squat-back-pain-and-triple-jump-takeoff-led-verkhoshansky-to-depth-jumps]] (the origin story in the same paper); [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]] (reactive ability); [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[principle--reserve-the-shock-method-for-experienced-top-level-athletes-not-youth]]

# How Depth Jumps Began: Heavy Half Squats Hurt His Jumpers' Backs, and Triple-Jump Take-Off Forces Pointed to a Shock Load Instead

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky's first-person account (PDF 574-575 / pp.563-564, checked against the page images). In the mid-1950s he coached high-level jumpers and was "a senior coach in the sprint and jump events in Moscow". He was "one of the first coaches in Russia to use a barbell" for athletes, with a first article in 1957; a main exercise was "the full barbell squat using a weight of 120 kg which gave good results." He then switched to the half squat "with much more barbell weight"; his athletes "could easily execute a half squat with 140-160 kg", but "the next day none of them came to train. They phoned me and told me about pain in the small of the back. I understood that that I had made a serious error in my strength training system" (PDF 574-575; "that that" is on the page). He then recalled his study of triple-jump take-off biodynamics (book published 1961): "the mean magnitude of dynamic effort in the take off for the second jump (step) is about 300-350 kg and lasts only 120 ms. In this instance the effort has a shock type of work when muscles are stretched very sharply and then are very quickly and very powerfully contracted." So he "decided that depth jumping, with landing and takeoff on both legs, would be an effective means of reactive ability improvement. Experiments have confirmed this hypothesis." The method spread through Fred Wilt and Michael Yessis (USA), Peter Tschiene (Germany), Mel Siff (South Africa) and Carmelo Bosco (Italy) (PDF 575 / p.564; the page prints "Carmello").

**Why it works** — His reasoning in the account: the sport's own key effort (300-350 kg in about 120 ms in the step take-off) is a sharp stretch followed by a fast, powerful contraction, which a heavy slow squat does not reproduce; a depth jump does, with body mass and fall height supplying the load instead of a bar on the spine. Inference: the same contrast appears in 5.2.4, where heavy squats are said to train mainly quasi-isometric strength and to place "a large and generally unnecessary load on the spine" ([[claim--heavy-squats-and-light-fast-lifts-miss-the-eccentric-concentric-switch]]).

**When to apply** — As a reasoning pattern: when a loaded exercise is chosen to raise a sport's peak force, compare its force and time with the sport's key action. Inference: his numbers say the step take-off load is about twice the heaviest half squat he used, delivered in roughly a tenth of a second, so heavier half squats chase the wrong target. Eric's baseline: training time is weighted toward "high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints)" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 104, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: his story is an argument for keeping jumps and shock work beside the squat in that mix, not for dropping the squat; he kept the full squat.

**When NOT to apply** — This is an anecdote. No athlete count, injury records or experiment details are given, and "Experiments have confirmed this hypothesis" has no data or citation on these pages. "300-350 kg" is a force stated in kilograms (kilogram-force) with no bodymass, so it cannot be turned into multiples of bodyweight here. The back pain followed one session of heavier half squats; the page does not say whether load, range, technique or the jump from 120 kg to 140-160 kg caused it. Do not read the story as evidence that half squats are unsafe in general.

**Example** — The step take-off in the triple jump: about 300-350 kg of mean effort over about 120 ms (PDF 575 / p.564).

**Related** — [[claim--shock-method-is-a-forced-shock-stretch-of-tensed-muscle-not-plyometrics]]; [[claim--heavy-squats-and-light-fast-lifts-miss-the-eccentric-concentric-switch]]; [[claim--depth-landings-from-2-to-3-2-m-produce-forces-over-20-times-bodyweight]]; [[case-study--triple-jumper-annual-cycle-two-strength-blocks-fig-8]]; [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]] (RC tracks triple-jump performance)

# Verkhoshansky's 12-Week Leg Program: Heavy Squats, Then Loaded Jumps and Interval Squats, Then Depth Jumps, Then Box Jumps

**What it is** — "Program to develop explosive strength and reactive ability of the leg muscles" (PDF 578-582 / pp.567-571; every number below was read from the page images, since the table OCR is unreliable). Twelve weeks, two sessions a week for weeks 1-8, then "From the 9th week on, from day 17 - 28, workouts are executed three times a week" (the table numbers these as sessions 17-28). Four means: depth jump; barbell squat; consecutive barbell jumps, either squat jumps with the bar on the shoulders ("thighs are at least parallel to the floor", underlined on the page) or barbell scissor-lunge jumps (Fig 19); and box jumps, "Consecutive jumps onto a box and down using a double leg takeoff", box "0.4 - 0.8 m" (Fig 20). Loads are % of squat 1RM; "8 x 10 (2)" means 2 series of 8 sets of 10 (PDF 578 / p.567). The phases:

| Weeks (sessions) | Content |
|---|---|
| 1-3 (1-6) | Squats only. Heavy days pair 90% or 93-95% (2-4 x 3-5 or 3-5 x 2-3, rest 4-6 min) with 80-85% volume sets (2-3 x 10-12 to 3-5 x 8-10); pyramid days (80% 1 x 10, 90% 1 x 5, 90-95% 1 x 2; or 70% 1 x 12, 80% 1 x 10, 85% 1 x 7) repeated 2-3 times |
| 4-5 (7-10) | Consecutive barbell jumps at 40%, 5 x 8 (2) then 8 x 8 (2), 60 s between sets; squats at 85-90% then 95% "using the interval method", 4-5 x 1-3 |
| 6-8 (11-16) | Depth jumps from 0.75 m and 1.10 m (2-4 x 10 in total per height pairing), 6-12 min rest, then barbell jumps at 40%, 6-10 sets of 8-10, set rest falling from 60 s to 30 s to 10 s |
| 9-11 (17-25) | Three sessions a week: two depth-jump days (4 x 10 from 1.10 m or 0.75 m, then barbell jumps 8-10 x 10 in 2-4 series) and one box-jump day (0.4-0.5 m 4 x 40 (2); 0.5-0.6 m 6 x 40 (2); 0.7-0.8 m 5 x 50 (3)) |
| 12 (26-28) | Barbell jumps 10 x 10 (3-4), 10 s between sets, twice; box jumps 0.7-0.8 m 6 x 50 (3), 2 min between sets |

Footnote 24: after the last 85% squat rep "it is necessary to do 2-3 additional repetitions" (PDF 579 / p.568). Footnote 25 defines the interval method (see [[framework--interval-resistance-training-and-cluster-sets]], Also in 9.2). The rules that follow the table are in [[heuristic--keep-the-order-of-means-and-reset-jump-load-to-40-percent-of-current-squat-max]].

**Recorded as printed (Inference: likely misprints):** sessions 12 and 13 list "Depth Jumps (0.10 m.)" as the second height, where every other session pairs 0.75 m with 1.10 m (PDF 580 / p.569); session 11 prints "8 x 10 (6)", six series, where every other barbell-jump row has 2 to 4 (PDF 580); the text says "day 17 - 28" for what the table calls training sessions (PDF 578).

**Why it works** — His stated principle, printed after the table: "gradually increasing the specificity and intensity of the training load", so "each training load prepares the organism for effective execution the following loads" (PDF 582 / p.571). Inference: the order (maximal strength first, then light loaded jumps, then depth jumps, then high-contact box jumps) matches the strength-first sequences reported in 5.3 and 6.9.1 ([[heuristic--sequence-jumps-then-barbell-then-depth-jumps-across-stages]], [[case-study--barbell-and-depth-jump-sequences-in-high-jumpers]]). The drop heights match the 0.75-1.15 m range of 4.2.3 ([[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]), with 1.10 m, not 1.15 m, as the high one.

**When to apply** — As a template for an off-season reactive block for jumpers or other leg-dominant power athletes who already squat heavily, keeping the phase order and the 40% barbell-jump load. Eric's baseline: "Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment within a training block" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)). Inference: the weeks 1-3 squat rows (for example 3-5 x 2-3 at 93-95%, 2 x 8 + 2-3 at 85%) can be checked against that chart before use.

**When NOT to apply** — No outcome data, population or sport is given for the program; it is a prescription. The contact counts are large: 10 x 10 barbell jumps in 3-4 series is 300-400 loaded jumps in a session, and 6 x 50 box jumps in 3 series is 900 contacts, which sits awkwardly beside his own rule that "It is the quality of the shock method, not the quantity that is important" (PDF 577 / p.566, item 7). Inference: the barbell and box jumps are submaximal rebound work, not shock-method depth jumps, which stay at 4 x 10 or less per session, within his item 2 cap (PDF 577). His conclusions restrict the shock method to "experienced top level athletes" (PDF 588 / p.577), so this is not a youth or novice program ([[principle--reserve-the-shock-method-for-experienced-top-level-athletes-not-youth]]). In-season football weeks do not fit a three-session-a-week reactive block (Inference).

**Example** — Session 16 (week 8): depth jumps 0.75 m 2 x 10 and 1.10 m 2 x 10, 6-8 min rest, then barbell jumps at 40% 8 x 10 in 2-3 series, 30 s between sets and 8-12 min between series (PDF 581 / p.570).

**Related** — [[heuristic--keep-the-order-of-means-and-reset-jump-load-to-40-percent-of-current-squat-max]]; [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]; [[heuristic--maximal-plyometric-and-depth-jump-volume-and-rest]]; [[claim--depth-jump-training-beat-higher-volume-traditional-training-in-jumpers]] (5.2.4, 475 depth jumps in 12 weeks); [[framework--interval-resistance-training-and-cluster-sets]]; [[case-study--six-week-starting-acceleration-program-squats-loaded-jumps-depth-jumps-bounds-hills]]
